disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are either not observable or appear slight to others, leading to significant distress or impairment. Individuals commonly engage in repetitive behaviors (such as mirror checking, grooming, or seeking reassurance) or mental acts in response to their concerns. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood and the course is often chronic, with symptoms waxing and waning around stressors, interpersonal situations, and appearance-related events. BDD is distinct from normal appearance concerns and from eating disorders in that the focus is on specific perceived defects rather than weight/shape globally, and from psychotic disorders in that beliefs, while sometimes overvalued, are usually not frankly delusional across contexts.

narrative.personality: Stephany is an imaginative, anxious, and highly conscientious young therapist who channels her creativity into art and writing while holding herself to very exacting standards.
narrative.stressor: Stephany’s concerns about how she looks began to intensify during her practicum and early clinical work, when supervisors and peers repeatedly emphasized professional image, video-recorded sessions for review, and commented casually on how "put together" a therapist should appear. Already self-critical and used to staying up late perfecting her notes and creative interventions, she started scrutinizing her appearance on camera before supervision, spending increasing amounts of time trying to control how she came across to clients and colleagues. As she transitioned into her community therapist role, the pressure of being the "calm, grounded" professional in front of clients, combined with social media images of other young therapists, made her feel that minor perceived flaws were incompatible with being credible and safe for patients. Over time, the effort she invested in managing these appearance worries began to erode her sleep, delay her arrival to sessions, and interfere with her ability to focus on clients, leading her to seek psychiatric help when she realized her own internal preoccupations were undermining the work she cared most about.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m getting stuck in these rituals around how I look before sessions, and it’s starting to take over my days.”

narrative.personality: Jessica is a sociable, meticulous organizer who enjoys being the energetic, well-put-together centerpiece of office and community life.
narrative.stressor: Around the time Jessica entered her early 60s, several transitions converged: colleagues began retiring, younger staff joined the office, and she started thinking seriously about her own "next chapter" while still working in a very visible administrative role for senior federal leadership. She had long taken pride in her appearance at work and on the ballroom dance floor, but the contrast between her and her much younger coworkers, along with frequent office photos and video calls, made her acutely aware of normal age-related changes she interpreted as glaring flaws. As she adjusted to friends moving away, more time alone at home, and the subtle shift from being the "young, glamorous" assistant to the "older" one, she increasingly invested time and mental energy into trying to control and disguise what she saw as unacceptable changes in how she looked. When her careful grooming routines, shopping for products, and preparation for social events began to make her late to work, sap her enjoyment of dancing and travel, and cause her to turn down invitations she once loved, she sought psychiatric evaluation at the urging of a close friend from her book club who noticed how preoccupied and distressed she had become about her appearance.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m spending way too much time fussing over how I look before work or going out, and it’s starting to interfere with everything I do.”

narrative.personality: James is a steady, service-oriented man who is thoughtful, dutiful, and tends to internalize stress while trying to be reliable for others.
narrative.stressor: In his mid-50s, James went through a period of health challenges, including weight fluctuation and treatment for a minor cardiac issue, which led to more frequent medical visits and advice about lifestyle changes. Seeing himself in clinic mirrors, patient portal photos, and ID badges after these changes, he began to fixate on specific aspects of his appearance that he felt made him look unwell or "damaged," and he compared himself harshly to old family photos he used in his genealogy hobby. Working in a customer service role where he is face-to-face with people all day and informally mentors younger staff, he started to feel that his perceived physical "defects" undermined his authority and the calm, competent image he prided himself on projecting. Over time, these worries began occupying more of his mental space at work and home, causing him to avoid certain social situations and feel increasingly distracted and exhausted, prompting him to seek psychiatric help after his spouse pointed out how much of his free time had become consumed by brooding over and trying to "fix" how he looks.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop zeroing in on what’s wrong with how I look since my health issues, and it’s really wearing me down.”
